utterances.text: Except being dead, the bodies showed signs of abuse. Their throats were cut and their eyes were slit out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had there been anything else done to the bodies? Had there been any sexual assaults on the bodies that you could see?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: On two bodies, the genitals were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know or ascertain the ethnic background or nationality of these policemen?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, prior to the actual outbreak of hostilities in the Vukovar region, did you have occasion to see Mr. Dokmanovic in the town of Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of how it is that you came to see him there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: In the beginning of August, I received an invitation from a family whose son was an invalid, a six-year-old, and I was called to treat him. So I went, and my wife accompanied me, and also because I had many friends there. So I reached the barricades at the entrance to Trpinja and I was allowed to pass. I went to examine the boy, and many citizens of Trpinja found out -- learned that I was there and invited me to help them too. On my way back, I dropped in on a friend, and on my way back from Trpinja, I met Dokmanovic, who was escorted by other persons, several other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, where did you see him? Where did you see Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It was right in central Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was this? What date, approximately, as best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It was the first week of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was Mr. Dokmanovic doing, anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, I think he was together with four or five people who were armed but in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was Mr. Dokmanovic dressed at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: He was dressed in drab olive trousers and a shirt of a slightly lighter colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise these clothes as being of any particular type?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They were usually worn by the reserve force, the reservists. The reservists keep these uniforms, keep this clothing at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this uniform a plain colour or was it what is often known as camouflage?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It was plain, plain olive in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Mr. Dokmanovic armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what do you mean when you said that he was being escorted? What did you mean by that statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Well, these were people from Trpinja, armed. Some were dressed in civilian clothes, some wore military clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ascertain what the relationship between them and Mr. Dokmanovic was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Well, the relationship, those people were escorting him because he was the president of the local community there. And later on, he was the president of the municipality, the municipal assembly in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So when you say "escorted," you're not suggesting he was their prisoner or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, no. He came to talk to me. We exchanged hellos. I recognised one of those people and I said hello to him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who appeared to be the person in charge of the group, as such, if I could put it that way?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I think he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What discussion did you have with him? Was it just a social discussion or can you recall?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: He asked me how I was. He told me to say hello to my wife. I asked him about the conditions of life and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you seen Mr. Dokmanovic dressed in this way before?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, never. He was always in civilian clothes, a suit and a tie. He was never dressed like that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you ask him why he was dressed this way or have any conversation with him because he was -- about this matter?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, I never had any discussions about politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of the war, where did you stay? This is during --

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: In Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay there for how long, right up until what date?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I remained in Borovo Naselje from July '82 until the end of the war when I was captured on the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when were you captured in November of 1991? My question is: What date in November 1991 were you captured?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you captured?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: In the factory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. I didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The New Shoes factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where is the New Shoes factory? Where is it located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: In the centre of Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who captured you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say they captured you, why did they capture you; do you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They captured everybody there, the entire population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they captured you, what did they do with you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They separated the men from the women. Then all the men above the age of 14 were put on buses and we were all taken to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where is Vojvodina? In what republic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: In Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What part of Vojvodina were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Near the town of Zrenjanin. It was a farm. It was a farm in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to this place, Zrenjanin, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: We were there. There were about 20 buses. The buses stopped about 20 metres away from the entrance. And as we got out, we had to pass through a gauntlet of people who beat us all the way to the entrance to the cattle barns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who were the people that beat you as you ran through the gauntlet to the entrance?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The military police, civilian police, civilians who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The military and civilian police of where?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you ran through the guantlet, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They beat us from both sides with rifle butts and batons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Then we were all gathered at the entrance and we had to sit down on the floor, put our heads down, hands behind our backs, and they beat us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, how long did you stay in this place, this farm?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: We arrived at around 9.00 p.m. until 3.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened at 3.00 a.m.? What happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Among us who were captured there, there were people of Serbian ethnic background who had remained in Borovo Naselje throughout the war. When we were being beaten, one of the captives, a Serb, started shouting "Why do you beat me? I'm a Serb just like you are." He was then asked to say his name and then he was allowed to go in. Then the other people also gathered courage. There were several more Serbs, and so it lasted until 3.00 a.m. Then nobody else said that they were Serbs. I thought that as a non-Yugoslav citizen, as a foreigner, I also thought that I should try my luck. I said, "I am a foreign citizen. I'm not a Yugoslav. I'm not a Croat." Then they asked me where I was from, and (redacted) that I lived (redacted). They said, "No, you are a mercenary." So they separated me from the group, put me in the other part of the shed, and five or six people started to beat me really hard. It lasted for about 20 minutes. Then they left me alone. After about 15 minutes, I saw a civilian. I only saw his legs and they were dressed in denims. I was unable to look up. He told me, he asked me, "Doctor, are you being beaten as well?" And he said, "Come with me. They will not beat you anymore." I thought that was a joke because he was in civilian clothes. Then he took me below my armpits and he mentioned my name, and he said, "Doctor, nobody is going to beat you anymore." I looked at him. He was a young man, about 25. And he looked at the major who was in charge, and he said that I should not be beaten anymore. And he took me inside the shed. That's where the Serb captives were held. I stood there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And then you were taken ultimately to another place?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I was there until the morning, and then the camp commander arrived, Colonel Zivanovic. The civilian talked to him, approached me, and said that there was a mistake, they didn't know who I was and, if possible, I should help them in the camp because there were quite a few wounded people among the prisoners, and they did not have any medical personnel. I said, "No problem, but I can't do it alone. There are other doctors among the captives." And he allowed me to look for them. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: nurses. So we were put in a separate part of the shed, given five blankets, and they said that this should be the medical unit, that we should be helping the detainees. That's how I started to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may seek a redaction at line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After about five days, after you had been in this camp -- no, I withdraw that, Your Honours. What was the nature of the camp that you worked at as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It was an old farm, and it seems that it was out of use for a long time. We were in the shed where pigs used to be kept. There were throws still there but there was no water. There were no windows, no electricity. When we arrived, the electricity was installed. We were there for seven days and we were unable to leave the room. There were about 1.500 of us and 200 more arrived later. There was no wire around. It took them seven days to put up the wire fence and to install a latrine. Until that time, we used a place behind the wall for our physical needs. For the first two days, nobody ate anything. A soldier brought some water on his shoulders, and then if a guard was in a good mood, would give the water to those people who were thirsty. If he was in a bad mood, he wouldn't give you any water. We slept on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was running this camp?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With what organisation was he involved and with what organisation was he attached to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Military police of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was the JNA police establishment, was it, a military police establishment?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After four or five days, did you see someone at the camp that you knew?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The third day, that was the first time when I was brought in for questioning, there was a small building outside the shed. It was probably some kind of an office while the farm was in operation. There were several offices there. I went there three days in a row to be questioned. I think on the fourth or on the fifth day when I was in the camp, after the interrogation at around 11, when I was brought into the corridor, I met Mr. Dokmanovic and four other people who were in his escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was Mr. Dokmanovic dressed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: He was wearing a military -- a pair of military trousers, dark green, and on top, he had some kind of a jacket, a military jacket of a plain colour. It was short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, was the whole uniform of a plain colour or was there any part of his uniform which was of the camouflage sort?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It wasn't a camouflage. It was a plain colour uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he armed on the occasion that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The jacket was zipped up so I couldn't see any arms or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the people that were with him, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They wore camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise whether or not they were a part of any military establishment, as such, from the way they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They did not have any insignia on their caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they wearing caps?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Some, some had caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they have arms? Were they carrying any arms?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were the rifles of the military type or the civilian type of hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, when you saw these people with Mr. Dokmanovic, did they, again, appear to be escorting him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, they walked behind him. He was right at the front, the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you gain any impression as to his position vis-à-vis or with respect to the other people that he was with?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What impression was that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Well, that he was in charge, that he was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you saw Mr. Dokmanovic, did you get a clear view of him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, the corridor was about a metre and a half wide, and we passed each other by. I was getting out of the corridor; he was getting in. When he saw me, he turned his head away, as if I didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think that he saw you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why are you 100 per cent sure that he saw you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Because at that moment, I was there with my guard leading me out, and he was getting in. There was no other choice. This was a rather narrow corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attempt to speak to him? I'm afraid your answer hasn't appeared on the transcript, so could you answer that question? Did you attempt to speak to him? You need to speak up.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why didn't you attempt to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I was a detainee and I was not allowed to do anything without permission, because we were beaten when we disobeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you feel when you saw Mr. Dokmanovic? What was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I was disappointed, sorely disappointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why were you disappointed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I was disappointed because, as a friend, he knew that I was a foreign national. He knew that I had remained there purely in the capacity of a doctor, and he could have helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why do you say that he could have helped you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Well, as the mayor of Vukovar, he must have had some influence, if nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not he was the mayor of Vukovar at that time, that particular time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: From the very first day when we arrived in the camp, they let us listen to Serbian news on the radio. So when I was in the camp, I heard who was the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who was that? Who was it that you heard was the mayor of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I want you to have a look at some still photographs that are taken off a video that's been tendered as an exhibit in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an extract from video D2. Perhaps one of the photographs could be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph is marked 254.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could I have one copy back, please? I think I've given up my only copy. Oh, I'm sorry, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness R, just looking at the photograph beside you there, you see two gentlemen; one which appears, obviously, I think, in civilian clothes; you'd agree? Just look beside you there. Do you recognise the uniform worn by the gentleman on the left-hand side of the photograph, looking at the photograph?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is that uniform that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It's a military drab olive uniform, grey/olive colour, worn by the JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to look at this photograph. Just leave that one there for the moment and look at this photograph which is shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, this is an extract of D2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Photograph is marked 255.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Witness R, would you just quickly look for a moment, please, at the photograph that's displayed beside you there? Do you see the gentleman in the photograph which is closest to you on the left-hand side of the photograph, looking at the photograph? Is that the sort of uniform that you saw Mr. Dokmanovic in on two occasions that you saw him, one in Trpinja and then ultimately in the camp?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, the top was a plain colour, olive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of the two uniforms that I've shown you, both on Exhibit 254 and 255, what was the uniform most like the one that you saw him wearing in Trpinja in August and ultimately in the camp when you were there at the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The first picture, with the exception of the top, because the top was -- he wore a short coat on top. It was a plain colour with a zipper front.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, during the course of time that you knew Mr. Dokmanovic, ever have occasion to hear him speak about political views and his views of Croatian people and other nationalities during the period leading up to 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, I did have occasion, mostly 1990. I was invited to the celebration of the anniversary of the club. And certain songs, nationalistic songs, were being sung.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you gain any impression as to Mr. Dokmanovic's views on nationalistic matters?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Serbian, because the songs were Serbian, and they were about greater Serbia and the king and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you have any view about or any opinion about his views? Were they moderate, reserved, or were they extreme?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Extreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Doctor, I think that during the course of the war, your wife tragically died; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that very recently her body has been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Fifteen days ago, I was in Vukovar, and we found her in the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately how many bodies were in this mass grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Finally, could you look around the courtroom and see if you can see Mr. Dokmanovic in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I can see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please point to him and describe where he is located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: He's wearing a grey suit, a white shirt, and he's sitting way back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the witness was identified, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Take your time. We can go on on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Witness R -- is it R? Yes. Witness R, you said that on two occasions, you saw Mr. Dokmanovic wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that he had the same uniform both times.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It says that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I said in August he was wearing the shirt and the trousers. That's correct. In the camp, he was wearing a jacket, a plain-coloured jacket with a zippered front.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it a military jacket?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Che Guevara type of jacket, the field marshall type of jacket. American officers still wear that kind of jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but was it the uniform of the reservists that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The first one was the reservist uniform. The second one was just in addition because it was cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the first time, you saw him in a reservist uniform?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And in December?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It was the same thing. The same trousers, dark green, and then on top he had this jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's not the reservist JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to know. Did I understand you correctly that you said that this reservist uniform was the kind of uniform that was issued after serving national service, to take home?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: There were two kinds. I was very much familiar with it. There was a first type with the long overcoat, and then later on, instead of the overcoat, there was a plain-coloured uniform with pockets on the sides. It was green for soldiers, and for officers -- for policemen it was bluish.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. The question is: Is that the kind of uniform that we were issued after doing our national service to take home?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but it was not the full uniform because it was summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he only had the shirt and the trousers. You said that you were a family friend of Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who are the members of his family?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Brother, who used to work for me; his wife, I was her doctor; his brother's wife, I used to visit his house, and in '85, when he started building his house, I was there every week. He was the President of the Sindelic soccer club. I was there as a doctor every Sunday, every week. After the matches, we would go to celebrate. We sat together.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you visit him at home?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he a good host?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you saw him in the village that time, was it inside Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please describe it in more detail? He was in a uniform, as you described, a shirt and trousers, and he was there with some other people who were dressed in a different manner. What does it mean, "in a different manner"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Some had some parts of uniform and others were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he doing with them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They were walking around. He was talking to them. In the centre of the city, in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were they in his escort as bodyguards or were they simply accompanying him as friends? What use did he have about the guards in the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I don't think he needed bodyguards there, but those were his boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: His friends. What were they, his countrymen from Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, from Trpinja. Some of them were soccer players from his club, and I can mention one of them who talked to him and his name was Savo Prodanovic. I also knew him, but I can't remember. He was from the club of Luzani, he was also with them, this other person whose name I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please speak more slowly? Please tell the counsel and the witness to make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you make a difference between people who are accompanying somebody like president of the club with his players or you with your patients and the situation when somebody is escorting somebody like the entourage of a statesman?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I think they were escorting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In which sense?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: As his army. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But he did not have arms?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know what was the business of Savo Prodanovic in Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know if he was from Trpinja or from the village of Dalj?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where he came from. I know that he played in Trpinja and that's where I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that club in Trpinja, did Croats play soccer there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes. I already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did he ever come to accept Croats if he was extreme?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: That was '83-'84.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He was not extreme then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They sang songs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, both of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you mean the song, "Who says that Serbia is small?"

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You believe that is a nationalist song?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: It was not pro-Yugoslav anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when Croats sang such songs, national songs, you thought they were extreme?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They were nationalistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You, as far as I understood, believe that because the corridor is narrow, he must have seen you. You did not exchange glances.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: He must have seen me because each of us had to move to avoid the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that's your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You knew that in a certain period he became president of the Municipal Assembly, in other words, mayor of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You know he was mayor, but you don't know whether he was president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Maybe before the war. I didn't follow politics very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When was he president of the local community?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: While I was in the soccer club, '83-'84.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did he become mayor of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I don't know. Don't ask me. I know that after the war, he was mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you know that he became mayor after the war, and you don't know whether he was mayor before the war.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I didn't follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you hear on the radio when you found out that he was mayor?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: We heard about the complete government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You heard about the government. Did you hear that he was Minister?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You heard about some government?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was he on that government?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: He was mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the government?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was he on that government?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your friendship, did he say anything bad to you because you're obviously not a Serb?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he display any hostilities towards you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Except for singing those songs in the soccer club, as far as I understood. Did you notice anything else about him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he say anything bad to anybody else in your presence?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No. Well, you know that we were in Trpinja, which is 100 per cent Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you say that Croats played soccer.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, but villages played between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is simple: Did Slavko Dokmanovic ever, in your presence, say anything bad about somebody who was not a Serb?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes. In 1990. I was invited to the anniversary of the club and I received some sort of token of gratitude from the club, and on that occasion, they sung very nasty songs against Croats, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We understood that much. But did he personally say anything?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: If he was the one who organised those celebrations and if he allowed them to sing such songs, then he must have held such views. He was the organiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understand. You mean that he was president of the club, and during the celebration of the anniversary, somebody sang nationalist songs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Not anyone but everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But apart from that singing, did you ever hear him, in your presence, say anything bad?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: What do you mean? To whom could he say that if they -- they were mostly Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On that anniversary; that was the only occasion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: To them, I'm a foreigner. I'm not a Croat and I'm not a Serbian either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see Dokmanovic, did you meet with Dokmanovic ever outside Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No, only in Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then I apologise because I thought you saw him outside Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I met with Slavko every week or every other week but in Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know who Pavle Maric is? Was he president of that club?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 1991, who was president?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: The last five years, I did not spend in that club, and I didn't even work there as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean you were just at the anniversary?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes. I was there to receive that token of gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know whether Pavle Maric was then president of the club?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: I don't know. While I was there as a doctor, he was president.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you don't know who was president in 1990?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No. I saw only Dokmanovic. He thanked me as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know what he said in his speech? Did he thank you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Yes, he thanked me for my efforts and my contribution to their success.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that speech, there were no nationalist notes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could I have, please, Prosecution Exhibit D2 -- no, 48, please? Could you just show him the shirt and the trousers? Does he recognise any of those clothes as worn by Slavko Dokmanovic on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It's a Defence Exhibit. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I've been asking questions and mentioning exhibits all day long, so I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Witness, of all these things I'm going to show you, did Mr. Dokmanovic wear any of these things on the first or on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: [Shown item of clothing] No. [Shown item of clothing] No. [Shown jacket] On the second occasion, he wore something similar but shorter and lighter in colour with a zipper. It was the second occasion, when it was winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, the last question: On the second occasion you saw him, that was outside the building of the camp?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No. Outside the casualty shed, there was a building serving as offices, and there they held the interrogation of captives. I was leaving the interrogation through the corridor, one metre and a half wide, and he was facing me coming into the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On that occasion when you saw him, did he ever make an utterance, a command or anything to others?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No. He just looked the other way and people behind him kept talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he did not talk to people who were behind him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: No. They talked between themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you then conclude that they were escorting him? Perhaps they were just there by chance behind him.

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: They were following him. He was leading the way. The distance between them was so small that they could not have been separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So that's your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL TABBUSH
utterances.text: Well, you see it's not a promenade. Not anyone can enter simply and walk around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there is no -- yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am tired. Please don't mind my lapses. Your Honour, I received information from the Dutch police that perhaps the forensics of the tape will be finished by Saturday -- sorry, by Wednesday. If that is so, will that report suffice, or shall I bring the person in charge of the forensic analysis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I turn to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would have to read it, but subject to reading it, being satisfied that we have no problem with it being tendered that way, certainly we would be happy to do that, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us, first of all, read the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to read it as well if I receive it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I was about to ask whether there is an objection to the witness being released. There is no objection. So, Witness R, we thank you for coming here to give evidence, and you may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we will now rise and we will reconvene on Tuesday, next Tuesday, at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 5.03, to the reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of June, 1998, at 9.30 a.m. 25
